items.title: Lesson 1 "Infer" (Figure 1): Why are you more likely to get a shock from a metal doorknob after walking on a carpet on a cold, dry winter day than on a humid summer day?

body.html: Walking on carpet transfers charge to your body. The charge stays only if it cannot leak away. Dry air is a good insulator; humid air carries charge away.

In winter the air is dry, so the charge picked up from the carpet stays on you until you touch the knob, and then it jumps in a spark. In humid summer air, water in the air carries the charge away a little at a time, so little builds up.

answer.html: In dry air the charge collected by scuffing across the carpet cannot leak away, so it builds up and discharges as a shock; in humid air it drains off continuously and there is little left to shock you.

items.title: Lesson 1 "Get It?" (pen at the start of the module): A glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth and then attracts small bits of paper. Predict the type of charge on the rod and on the silk.

body.html: Glass tends to become positively charged when rubbed with silk. Charge is conserved, so the silk gains the opposite charge. A charged rod attracts neutral paper whichever its sign, so the paper alone does not tell the sign.
Silk holds electrons more strongly than glass does, so electrons move from the glass to the silk. The glass is left with a deficiency of electrons and the silk with an excess.

answer.html: The glass rod is positive and the silk is negative. The attraction of paper cannot confirm this, because it would occur for either sign.

items.title: Lesson 1 "Consider why electrical wires are coated with rubber" (Figure 4): Explain why the handles of an electrician's pliers are covered with plastic.

body.html: Metal is a conductor; plastic is an insulator.
The metal jaws carry charge easily. The plastic handle will not let charge pass, so current cannot travel from a live wire through the tool into the electrician's hand.

answer.html: Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps charge from flowing from the metal tool to the person, preventing shock.

items.title: 1 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): Two tape strips X and Y were charged by separation, so they carry opposite charges. A glass rod rubbed with silk is known to be positive. How could you find out which strip is negatively charged?

body.html: Use an object of known charge and the rule that like charges repel while unlike charges attract. Because X and Y are opposite, one will be repelled and the other attracted.
Bring each strip near the charged glass rod. The strip that is repelled has the same (positive) charge as the rod. The strip that is attracted has the opposite (negative) charge.

answer.html: Bring both strips near the positive glass rod. The strip that is attracted to the rod is the negatively charged one; the strip that is repelled is positive.

items.title: 2 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall in the evening but has fallen by the next morning. Explain why.

body.html: Excess charge stays on an insulator only until it can escape; air always has some moisture and ions.

Overnight the balloon's excess charge was carried away by water vapor, dust, and ions in the air, and passed into the wall where it touched. With no net charge left, there is nothing to polarize the wall and no attraction.

answer.html: The balloon's charge slowly leaked away into the air and wall, so it became neutral and the electrostatic attraction disappeared.

items.title: 3 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): A foam ball hangs from a thread, and you have only a rod known to be negatively charged. What can you conclude from how the ball responds, and what extra step is needed to decide between the possibilities?

body.html: Only repulsion proves a ball is charged with the same sign as the rod. A neutral ball and an oppositely charged ball are both attracted by the rod.

Bring the negative rod near the ball. If the ball is repelled, it must be negatively charged. If the ball is attracted, it is either neutral or positive. To decide, bring a rod of known positive charge (for example, glass rubbed with silk) near: a neutral ball is attracted to it, while a positive ball is repelled.

answer.html: Repulsion by the negative rod means the ball is negative. Attraction means it is neutral or positive, and a positive rod is needed to tell them apart (neutral is attracted by it, positive is repelled).

items.title: 4 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): A glass rod becomes positive when rubbed with silk. What happens to the charge of the silk, and why?

body.html: Charge is conserved; rubbing separates charge, it does not create it.
Electrons move from the glass to the silk. The glass loses 𝑛 electrons and the silk gains the same number.

answer.html: The silk becomes negatively charged, with a charge equal in magnitude to the rod's, because it gained the electrons the glass lost (conservation of charge).

items.title: 5 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): A basketball contains about 1025 charged particles, yet two basketballs lying near each other do not push or pull on each other. Why not?

body.html: Electrostatic forces depend on net charge. Ordinary matter has equal numbers of positive and negative charges.
Each ball has nearly as many protons as electrons, so its net charge is essentially zero. Any force from a positive particle is cancelled by that of a negative one.

answer.html: Each basketball is neutral, so its positive and negative charges balance and the net electrostatic force between the balls is essentially zero.

items.title: 6 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): A metal rod hangs from silk threads. A negatively charged rubber rod touches one end of it. Describe the charges on the metal rod afterward.

body.html: Rubber rubbed with fur is negative. Metal is a conductor with mobile electrons; silk is an insulator that isolates the rod.

Where the rubber rod touches, some of its excess electrons flow onto the metal. Electrons repel each other and move freely in metal, so they spread over the whole rod. The silk threads keep them from escaping.

answer.html: The metal rod ends up with a net negative charge spread over the entire rod, not just at the touched end.

items.title: 7 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): What happens when you hold an aluminum rod in your bare hand and rub it with fur?

body.html: Aluminum is a conductor, so charge does not stay in one place.
Electrons transferred by the rubbing spread through the rod and flow through your body into the ground. The rod cannot keep a net charge.

answer.html: The aluminum rod does not stay charged: the charge spreads out and drains through you to the ground. (With an insulating handle, it could keep a small charge.)

items.title: 8 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1): Give two observations that the two-charge model explains better than a single-fluid model.

body.html: A model is better if it explains more observations.

A single fluid (excess flows toward deficit) explains only attraction between a "full" and an "empty" object. Observation 1: Two rods that are both positive (both short of electrons) repel just as two negative rods do. The two-charge model says like charges repel whatever their sign. Observation 2: Neutral objects are attracted to charged objects of either sign. The two-charge model says neutral matter contains equal amounts of both charges, which can be separated. The two-charge model also matches the microscopic picture in which electrons move and the nuclei stay.

answer.html: The two-charge model explains (1) repulsion between two like-charged objects of either sign and (2) attraction of neutral objects by charges of either sign through charge separation, which the single-fluid model cannot.

items.title: Lesson 1 "Infer" (Figure 1) Question: Why would hair be more likely to stand up on a dry day than on a wet day?

body.html: Charge stays on hair and hat only if it cannot leak away. Dry air is a good insulator; humid air contains water molecules and droplets that pick up and carry charge away.
On a dry day the charge transferred by rubbing stays on each hair, so the hairs repel one another and are attracted to the hat. On a humid day the charge drains away into the moist air quickly.

answer.html: On a dry day the charge stays put (dry air insulates), so the electrostatic force is big enough to lift the hair; on a wet day the charge leaks away through the water in the air.

items.title: Lesson 1 "Get It?" (pen at the start of the module) Question: Predict the type of charge on the pen (rod) shown at the beginning of the module.

body.html: Hard rubber and plastic tend to become negatively charged when rubbed. Both signs of charge would attract the neutral water, so the water bending alone does not tell us the sign.
The rod is a plastic object that has been rubbed (probably on hair or clothing). Plastic gains electrons from the material it is rubbed on.

answer.html: Most likely negative (a plastic rod rubbed with cloth or hair gains electrons). The bending of the water cannot confirm this, because it would occur for either sign.

items.title: Lesson 1 "Consider why electrical wires are coated with rubber" (Figure 4)

body.html: Rubber is an insulator; metal is a conductor.

Charge moves easily along the metal wire but cannot move through rubber. The coating keeps the moving charge inside the wire and keeps you (and neighboring wires) from becoming part of the conducting path.

answer.html: Rubber is an insulator, so it keeps charge in the wire and protects people and other conductors from shock or short circuits.

items.title: 1 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: In the tape investigations, how could you find out which strip, B or T, is positively charged?

body.html: Use an object whose charge sign is known, and use the rule that like charges repel while unlike charges attract. Repulsion is the only definite test, because an attraction can also occur with a neutral object.

The book states that a plastic comb rubbed on clothing becomes negative. Bring each strip near the rubbed comb. The strip that is repelled has the same (negative) charge as the comb. The strip that is attracted has the opposite charge. (B and T were charged by separation, so they carry opposite charges.)

answer.html: Bring both strips near a rubbed plastic comb (known negative). The strip that is attracted to the comb is the positively charged one; the strip that is repelled is negative.

items.title: 2 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: Why does a rubbed comb lose its ability to pick up paper after a few minutes?

body.html: Charge on an insulator stays where it is only as long as it has nowhere to go; real air always contains some moisture and ions.

Over time the comb's excess electrons are carried off by water vapor, dust, and ions in the air (and by contact with the paper and your hand). When the comb is neutral again, there is no net charge to polarize the paper.

answer.html: The comb's excess charge slowly leaks into the surrounding air (and objects it touches), so it returns to neutral and no longer attracts the paper.

items.title: 3 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: How can you tell whether a hanging pith ball is neutral, positive, or negative?

body.html: Only repulsion proves the ball is charged with the same sign as the test rod. A neutral ball is attracted to a charged rod of either sign (by polarization).

Bring a rod of known negative charge near the ball, then a rod of known positive charge (for example, glass rubbed with silk). Attracted to both rods: ball is neutral. Repelled by the negative rod and attracted to the positive rod: ball is negative. Repelled by the positive rod and attracted to the negative rod: ball is positive.

answer.html: Test the ball with rods of known positive and negative charge. Attracted to both means neutral; repelled by a rod means it has the same sign as that rod.

items.title: 4 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: A rubber rod becomes negative when rubbed with wool. What happens to the charge of the

body.html: Charge is conserved; rubbing separates charge, it does not create it.
Electrons move from the wool to the rubber. The rod gains 𝑛 electrons; the wool loses the same number, leaving it with a deficiency of electrons.

answer.html: The wool becomes positively charged, with a charge equal in magnitude to the rod's, because the electrons the rod gained came from the wool (conservation of charge).

items.title: 5 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: An apple holds about 1026 charged particles. Why don't two apples repel each other?

body.html: Electrostatic forces depend on the net charge. Ordinary matter has equal numbers of positive and negative charges.
Each apple has about as many protons as electrons, so its net charge is essentially zero. Each charged particle's force is cancelled by an equal and opposite one from a charge of opposite sign.

answer.html: Each apple is neutral: its positive and negative charges balance, so the net electrostatic force between the apples is essentially zero.

items.title: 6 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: A metal rod hangs from silk threads. A charged glass rod touches one end of it. Describe the

body.html: Glass is positively charged (the book says glass tends to become positive). Metal is a conductor with mobile electrons; silk is an insulator that keeps the rod isolated.

Where the glass rod touches, electrons from the metal flow onto the positive glass, leaving the metal rod with a deficiency of electrons. Because electrons move freely in the metal, the remaining positive charge spreads over the whole rod. The silk thread prevents charge from escaping.

answer.html: The metal rod ends up with a net positive charge spread over the entire rod (not just at the touched end).

items.title: 7 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: What happens when you rub a copper rod with wool?

body.html: Copper is a conductor, so charge does not stay localized.
Any electrons transferred in rubbing spread through the rod and, if you hold the rod in your hand, flow through your body to the ground. So the rod does not stay charged.

answer.html: A copper rod held in the hand does not keep a net charge: charge spreads out and drains through you to the ground. (If the rod were held by an insulating handle, it could keep a small charge.)

items.title: 8 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 1) Question: How is the two-charge model more accurate than the single-fluid model?

body.html: A model is better if it explains more observations.

A single fluid (excess flows toward deficit) can explain only attraction between "full" and "empty" objects. It cannot explain why two objects that both have a deficit (for example, two glass rods) repel just as two objects with an excess do, or why neutral objects can be attracted by either kind of charged object. The two-charge model explains all of these: there are two kinds of charge, like charges repel, unlike attract, neutral objects hold equal amounts of both, and charges can be separated. It also matches the microscopic picture (negative electrons move; positive nuclei stay).

answer.html: The two-charge model (positive and negative, with equal amounts in neutral matter) explains repulsion between like charges of either sign, attraction of neutral objects by polarization, and the microscopic transfer of electrons, none of which the single-fluid model explains.
